q: Sales budgets are usually prepared product-wise, territory-wise and customer-wise mainly in order to:

options.A: Determine the cost of production of each product
options.B: Decide the credit period to be allowed by the suppliers
options.C: Fix the responsibility for achieving the sales targets on the respective areas and salesmen, and to compare the actual sales of each segment with its budget
options.D: Compute the amount of depreciation on the sales office assets

e: Breaking the sales budget down product-wise, territory-wise and customer-wise fixes responsibility for each segment's target on the respective areas and salesmen. Actual sales of each segment can then be compared with its budget for control.

q: The research and development budget of an enterprise is characterised by the fact that it:

options.A: Is drawn up for specific research projects approved by the top management, the amounts being sanctioned for each project, since the outcome of research is uncertain and its benefits arise over a long period
options.B: Is derived from the production budget by applying a standard research cost per unit of output
options.C: Varies directly with the output in the same way as the direct material cost
options.D: Is prepared only after the results of the research have been obtained

e: Research and development is budgeted project-wise, with amounts sanctioned for each specific project approved by top management. Research outcomes are uncertain and benefits arise over a long period, so it cannot be derived mechanically from output like a variable production cost.

q: The administrative overhead budget of an enterprise covers:

options.A: The wages of the workers engaged directly on production
options.B: The commission payable to the salesmen of the enterprise
options.C: The cost of power and lighting consumed inside the factory
options.D: The costs of general administration, such as office salaries, office rent, insurance, stationery and depreciation of office equipment, which are largely fixed in nature

e: The administrative overhead budget covers the costs of general administration, such as office salaries, office rent, insurance, stationery and depreciation of office equipment. These costs are largely fixed in nature and are distinct from factory and selling overheads.

q: A sale is made on credit in March and the cash is collected from the customer in May. The sale is recognised in the budgeted profit and loss account in March. In the cash budget, this sale will appear:

options.A: As a receipt in March itself, because that is when the sale is made
options.B: As a receipt in May, when the cash is actually collected, showing that the cash budget follows the timing of cash movement and not of income recognition
options.C: In neither March nor May, because credit sales are excluded from a cash budget
options.D: As a payment in May, when the customer is paid back

e: The cash budget records cash when it actually moves, not when income is recognised. A March credit sale collected in May therefore appears as a receipt in May, even though it is recognised in the budgeted profit and loss account of March.

q: For preparing a cash forecast covering a long period, the adjusted profit and loss method of preparing a cash budget may be used. Under this method, the starting point is:

options.A: The projected net profit for the period, which is then adjusted for non-cash items, changes in working capital, capital receipts and payments, tax and dividends to arrive at the expected cash position
options.B: The closing cash balance of the previous year, without any adjustment
options.C: The total of the sales budget for the period
options.D: The amount of the share capital of the enterprise

e: Under the adjusted profit and loss method, the starting point is the projected net profit for the period. It is then adjusted for non-cash items, changes in working capital, capital receipts and payments, tax and dividends to arrive at the expected cash position.

q: During the preparation of the budgets, fresh market information leads to the sales budget being revised upwards. The immediate consequence for the other budgets is that:

options.A: No other budget is affected, because each functional budget is independent
options.B: Only the cash budget needs to be revised, the production budget remaining unchanged
options.C: The production, materials purchase, labour and cash budgets must all be revised correspondingly, because the functional budgets are interdependent and are coordinated in the master budget
options.D: The master budget is abandoned and budgeting is started afresh in the next year

e: Functional budgets are interdependent and are coordinated through the master budget. An upward revision of the sales budget therefore requires corresponding revision of the production, materials purchase, labour and cash budgets, not of the cash budget alone.

q: A cash budget for a month shows an opening cash balance of Rs 25,000, estimated receipts of Rs 2,90,000 and estimated payments of Rs 3,50,000. The position at the end of the month will be:

options.A: An overdraft of Rs 60,000
options.B: A cash balance of Rs 35,000
options.C: An overdraft of Rs 35,000
options.D: A cash balance of Rs 65,000

e: Closing position = Rs 25,000 + Rs 2,90,000 - Rs 3,50,000 = Rs (-)35,000, that is an overdraft of Rs 35,000. Payments exceed the opening balance plus receipts, so the month ends with a bank overdraft.

q: The credit sales of an enterprise were Rs 3,00,000 in February and Rs 4,50,000 in March. Experience shows that 60% of the credit sales are collected in the month following the sale and the remaining 40% in the second month following. The cash to be received from debtors in April is:
e: Collections in April = 60 percent of March credit sales + 40 percent of February credit sales = 0.60 x Rs 4,50,000 + 0.40 x Rs 3,00,000 = Rs 2,70,000 + Rs 1,20,000 = Rs 3,90,000.

q: An enterprise purchases materials on credit. Its credit purchases were Rs 2,40,000 in March and Rs 3,20,000 in April. It pays its creditors 50% in the month of purchase and the remaining 50% in the following month. The cash to be paid to creditors in April is:
e: Payments in April = 50 percent of April purchases + 50 percent of March purchases = 0.50 x Rs 3,20,000 + 0.50 x Rs 2,40,000 = Rs 1,60,000 + Rs 1,20,000 = Rs 2,80,000.

q: For estimating its working capital by the components method, an enterprise expects to hold raw material stock of Rs 2,80,000, work-in-progress of Rs 1,20,000, finished goods of Rs 2,00,000, debtors of Rs 2,40,000 and a cash balance of Rs 60,000. Its expected current liabilities are creditors Rs 2,10,000, outstanding expenses Rs 70,000 and a bank overdraft of Rs 20,000. Its net working capital requirement is:
e: Current assets = Rs 2,80,000 + Rs 1,20,000 + Rs 2,00,000 + Rs 2,40,000 + Rs 60,000 = Rs 9,00,000. Current liabilities = Rs 2,10,000 + Rs 70,000 + Rs 20,000 = Rs 3,00,000, so net working capital = Rs 9,00,000 - Rs 3,00,000 = Rs 6,00,000.

q: The estimated sales of an enterprise for the coming year are Rs 48,00,000. On the basis of past experience, its working capital is estimated at 15% of the annual sales. The working capital required is:
e: Working capital by the percentage-of-sales method = 15 percent of Rs 48,00,000 = Rs 7,20,000. The estimate applies the historically observed working capital proportion to the expected annual sales.

q: The current assets of an enterprise are Rs 21,00,000 and its current ratio is 3.5 : 1. Its net working capital is:
e: Current liabilities = current assets / current ratio = Rs 21,00,000 / 3.5 = Rs 6,00,000. Net working capital = Rs 21,00,000 - Rs 6,00,000 = Rs 15,00,000.

q: In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are held for 35 days, the work-in-progress remains in process for 15 days, finished goods are held for 20 days and debtors are collected in 40 days. Suppliers allow 30 days' credit. The length of the net operating cycle is:

options.A: 80 days
options.B: 110 days
options.C: 140 days
options.D: 65 days

e: Net operating cycle = 35 + 15 + 20 + 40 - 30 = 80 days. The stockholding and debtor collection periods are added, and the credit period obtained from suppliers is deducted because suppliers finance that part of the cycle.

q: An enterprise shows negative working capital because a part of its fixed assets has been financed out of short-term funds. The main danger inherent in this position is:

options.A: That the enterprise will have to pay more income-tax
options.B: That its fixed assets will depreciate faster
options.C: That it will be unable to sell its products in the market
options.D: A serious liquidity risk, because if the short-term lenders and creditors press for payment, the enterprise cannot convert its fixed assets into cash quickly enough to meet them

e: Negative working capital means current liabilities finance part of the fixed assets, which cannot be converted into cash quickly. The danger is a liquidity crisis if short-term lenders and creditors press for payment, since only illiquid assets stand behind those dues.

q: Where no cash discount is offered by the suppliers, trade credit obtained on the usual terms is a particularly cheap source of short-term finance mainly because:

options.A: Within the credit period allowed, no explicit interest is charged on the amount owed, while the goods received can be used or sold before the payment falls due
options.B: The amount owed to the suppliers never has to be repaid
options.C: Trade credit is provided by the Government at a subsidised rate of interest
options.D: Suppliers allow the buyer to fix his own date of payment, without any limit

e: Where no cash discount is offered, trade credit costs nothing explicitly within the credit period allowed, as no interest is charged on the amount owed. The buyer can meanwhile use or sell the goods received before payment falls due, making it a cheap source of finance.

q: Outstanding or accrued expenses, such as wages, salaries, rent and interest that have become due but have not yet been paid, help in financing the working capital of an enterprise because:

options.A: Such expenses are never required to be paid at all
options.B: The bank pays these expenses on behalf of the enterprise
options.C: The enterprise first uses the services concerned and pays for them later, so that the amounts remaining payable act as an interest-free short-term source of funds until the due date of payment
options.D: Accrued expenses are a part of the share capital of the enterprise

e: Accrued expenses are services already used but not yet paid for, such as wages, rent and interest due. The amounts remaining payable act as an interest-free short-term source of funds until the payment date, thereby helping to finance working capital.

q: An enterprise borrows Rs 8,00,000 from a bank at 12% per annum interest, but is required to keep 10% of the loan amount as a compensating balance in its account with the bank, which it cannot use. The effective rate of interest on the funds actually available to it is:
e: Funds actually usable = Rs 8,00,000 - 10 percent compensating balance = Rs 7,20,000. Interest = 12 percent of Rs 8,00,000 = Rs 96,000, so the effective rate = Rs 96,000 / Rs 7,20,000 x 100 = 13.33 percent.

q: In the cash credit system of bank finance for working capital, the 'drawing power' of a borrower means:

options.A: The total limit sanctioned by the bank, which the borrower may draw in full at any time
options.B: The amount of the borrower's own contribution to the working capital
options.C: The profit that the borrower is expected to earn during the year
options.D: The amount computed on the value of the security, namely the paid-for stocks and book debts, after deducting the prescribed margin, the actual drawings being restricted to the lower of the sanctioned limit and the drawing power

e: Drawing power is computed on the value of the security, namely paid-for stocks and book debts, after deducting the prescribed margin. Actual drawings under cash credit are restricted to the lower of the sanctioned limit and the drawing power, not the full limit automatically.

q: A letter of credit opened by a bank at the request of a buyer of goods is, in the context of trade and working capital finance:

options.A: A loan of cash advanced by the bank to the buyer for paying the supplier
options.B: A written undertaking of the bank to the supplier or beneficiary to pay against the stipulated documents, being a non-fund-based facility which assures the seller of payment and enables the buyer to obtain the goods
options.C: A guarantee given by the supplier to the buyer about the quality of the goods
options.D: A bill of exchange drawn by the buyer on his bank

e: A letter of credit is the bank's written undertaking to the supplier or beneficiary to pay against the stipulated documents. It is a non-fund-based facility: it assures the seller of payment and enables the buyer to obtain the goods without an immediate cash loan.

q: The ageing schedule of the receivables of an enterprise shows, over successive months, a steadily increasing proportion of the total debtors falling in the oldest age groups. This trend primarily indicates that:

options.A: The quality of the receivables is deteriorating and collections are becoming slower, calling for stricter follow-up and possibly a tightening of credit
options.B: The sales of the enterprise are falling rapidly
options.C: The enterprise is collecting its debts faster than before
options.D: The suppliers of the enterprise have lengthened their credit period

e: An ageing schedule with a steadily rising share of debtors in the oldest age groups shows collections becoming slower and receivable quality deteriorating. It calls for stricter follow-up of overdue accounts and possibly a tightening of credit policy.

q: Under the credit scoring system of evaluating a credit applicant, the decision to grant credit is taken by:

options.A: Visiting the applicant's premises in every case and forming a personal impression
options.B: Scoring the applicant on characteristics such as income, occupation, length of service and past payment record, by means of a statistical scoring model, and comparing the total score with a pre-determined cut-off score
options.C: Asking the other suppliers of the applicant for their opinion in every case
options.D: Granting credit to every applicant who applies for it

e: Under credit scoring, the applicant is scored on characteristics such as income, occupation, length of service and past payment record using a statistical model. Credit is granted or refused by comparing the total score with a pre-determined cut-off score.

q: A stores item is classified as 'Vital' under the VED system of inventory control in a production unit. The correct stocking policy for such an item is that:

options.A: It should be stocked strictly according to its annual consumption value, like a low-value item
options.B: An adequate safety stock should be maintained so that a stock-out is virtually ruled out, even if the item is of low value, because its non-availability would halt production
options.C: No stock of it should be kept at all, to save working capital
options.D: It should be ordered only after the production has stopped for want of it

e: A Vital item under VED analysis is one whose non-availability would halt production. It must therefore carry an adequate safety stock so that a stock-out is virtually ruled out, even if the item is of low value; classification here rests on criticality, not consumption value.

q: The chief use of FSN analysis in the management of working capital is to:

options.A: Fix the selling prices of the finished products
options.B: Determine the credit period to be allowed to the customers
options.C: Compute the depreciation on the stores items
options.D: Identify the non-moving and slow-moving items of stock so that they can be reviewed and disposed of, releasing the funds unnecessarily blocked in obsolete stock

e: FSN analysis classifies stores into fast-moving, slow-moving and non-moving items. Its chief use is to identify non-moving and slow-moving stock for review and disposal, releasing funds unnecessarily blocked in obsolete inventory.

q: Where an enterprise adopts just-in-time purchasing, receiving materials in small and frequent lots timed to the needs of production, the effect on its working capital is that:

options.A: The average inventory held and the funds locked up in stock fall sharply, provided the suppliers are dependable and the delivery lead times are short and reliable
options.B: The inventory held rises, because deliveries are made more frequently
options.C: There is no effect at all on the working capital
options.D: The enterprise must pay for the whole year's material in advance

e: Just-in-time purchasing brings materials in small, frequent lots timed to production needs, so average inventory and the funds locked up in stock fall sharply. The benefit depends on dependable suppliers and short, reliable delivery lead times.

q: Even though the physical volume of its production and sales remains unchanged, an enterprise will require more working capital when the prices of its materials and its wage rates rise, mainly because:

options.A: Its fixed assets become more valuable in the market
options.B: Its suppliers stop supplying materials to it
options.C: A larger amount of funds gets locked up in each unit of stock held and in the debtors outstanding, since these are valued at the higher prices
options.D: The period of credit allowed by its suppliers becomes longer

e: With higher material prices and wage rates, each unit of stock held and each debtor outstanding is valued at a higher amount. More funds are therefore locked up in the same physical volume of operations, so the working capital requirement rises even though output is unchanged.

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 3,60,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 55,000 and a loss of Rs 12,000 on the sale of furniture, and after crediting interest of Rs 15,000 received on its investments. The funds from operations are:
e: Funds from operations = Rs 3,60,000 + Rs 55,000 depreciation + Rs 12,000 loss on sale - Rs 15,000 investment interest = Rs 4,12,000. Non-cash and non-operating charges are added back and non-operating income is deducted from net profit.

q: In preparing a fund flow statement, the proposed dividend is treated as a non-current liability. On this basis, the correct treatment of the dividend is:

options.A: Both the provision made and the dividend paid are ignored in the statement
options.B: The proposed dividend is shown as a source of funds
options.C: The provision for proposed dividend made during the year is added back to the profits in computing the funds from operations, and the proposed dividend of the previous year actually paid during the year is shown as an application of funds
options.D: The dividend paid is deducted in computing the funds from operations and is not shown elsewhere

e: The provision for proposed dividend made during the year is added back to profits in computing funds from operations, since proposed dividend is treated as a non-current liability. The previous year's proposed dividend actually paid during the year is shown as an application of funds.

q: An enterprise pays cash for purchasing the goodwill of another business. In its fund flow statement, this payment will be shown as:

options.A: An application of funds, being the acquisition of a non-current asset, namely an intangible asset
options.B: A source of funds, because goodwill increases the value of the business
options.C: An operating expense to be deducted in computing the funds from operations only, with no other entry
options.D: No entry at all, because goodwill is an intangible asset

e: Paying cash to acquire goodwill is the purchase of a non-current, intangible asset. In a fund flow statement such a payment is an application of funds, just like the purchase of any other fixed asset.

q: The debentures of an enterprise are redeemed at a premium, the premium being charged in the profit and loss account. The correct treatment of this premium in the fund flow statement is:

options.A: The premium is shown as a separate source of funds
options.B: The premium is ignored altogether in the statement
options.C: Only the premium is shown as an application of funds, and not the amount of the debentures
options.D: The premium charged to the profit and loss account is added back in computing the funds from operations, and the total amount paid on redemption, including the premium, is shown as an application of funds

e: The redemption premium charged to the profit and loss account is added back in computing funds from operations, because it is part of the redemption payment. The total amount paid on redemption, face value plus premium, is then shown as an application of funds.

q: Preliminary expenses and share issue expenses written off in the profit and loss account during a year are added back in computing the funds from operations because:

options.A: They represent cash actually received during the year
options.B: They are only the writing-off of fictitious or deferred assets on which the expenditure was incurred in an earlier year, and no funds move out of the enterprise in the year of the write-off
options.C: They are a part of the dividend declared during the year
options.D: They increase the working capital of the enterprise directly

e: Write-offs of preliminary and share issue expenses are added back because no funds move out in the year of write-off. The expenditure was incurred in an earlier year; the current entry merely writes down a fictitious or deferred asset in the books.

q: Underwriting commission, in connection with the issue of shares or debentures by a company, is:

options.A: The commission paid to underwriters for guaranteeing the subscription of the shares or debentures issued, being a cost of raising capital and of a capital nature
options.B: The commission paid to the selling agents on the sale of the products of the company
options.C: The brokerage paid by an investor for purchasing shares in the stock market
options.D: The commission charged by a bank for collecting the bills of the company

e: Underwriting commission is paid to underwriters for guaranteeing subscription of the shares or debentures issued, so that the issue succeeds even if the public does not fully subscribe. It is a cost of raising capital and is capital in nature.

q: For a financial enterprise such as a bank or a non-banking finance company, the cash flows arising from the loans and advances made by it to its customers are classified in its cash flow statement under AS-3 as cash flows from:

options.A: Investing activities, in every case
options.B: Financing activities, in every case
options.C: Operating activities, since lending is its principal revenue-producing activity
options.D: No activity, because loans are not cash flows

e: For a bank or finance company, lending is its principal revenue-producing activity, not an investment of surplus funds. Cash flows from its loans and advances are therefore classified under operating activities in its cash flow statement under AS-3.

q: Under AS-3, cash flows arising from extraordinary items, such as the proceeds of an insurance claim for a loss by fire, are dealt with in the cash flow statement by:

options.A: Omitting them from the statement altogether
options.B: Showing them always under operating activities, whatever their nature
options.C: Showing them always under financing activities
options.D: Classifying them as operating, investing or financing cash flows according to the nature of the item concerned, and disclosing them separately

e: Extraordinary items are classified as operating, investing or financing cash flows according to the nature of the item concerned, and are disclosed separately. An insurance claim for a fire loss, for example, follows the nature of the loss it compensates.

q: In preparing a cash flow statement, cash flows arising in a foreign currency are to be recorded:

options.A: At the exchange rate ruling on the date of the balance sheet in every case
options.B: At the exchange rate on the date on which the cash flow occurs, and the unrealised gains or losses arising from changes in exchange rates are not cash flows
options.C: Only at the end of the year, after netting all the receipts and payments
options.D: At the rate at which the original contract was entered into, ignoring the actual rate

e: Foreign currency cash flows are recorded at the exchange rate on the date the cash flow occurs. Unrealised gains or losses from changes in exchange rates are not cash flows, since no cash has moved.

q: Which of the following qualifies as a 'cash equivalent' for the purpose of a cash flow statement?

options.A: Treasury bills with an original maturity of 91 days, held as a short-term investment of surplus cash
options.B: Equity shares of a listed company held as an investment
options.C: Government bonds with a maturity of five years held as an investment
options.D: The inventory of finished goods held for sale

e: Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash, with an original maturity of about three months or less. Treasury bills with an original maturity of 91 days held for surplus cash therefore qualify.

q: An enterprise acquires the assets of another enterprise by issuing its own shares, and in another transaction converts its debentures into equity shares. In its cash flow statement under AS-3, these transactions are:

options.A: Shown as investing and financing cash flows at the values of the transactions
options.B: Shown partly as operating cash flows
options.C: Excluded from the cash flow statement, because no cash is involved, and disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements
options.D: Shown as a reduction of the opening cash balance

e: Acquiring assets by issuing shares and converting debentures into shares involve no movement of cash. Such non-cash investing and financing transactions are excluded from the cash flow statement and disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements.

q: An enterprise transfers a part of its bank balance into short-term money market instruments which qualify as cash equivalents, and later transfers the money back into its bank account. In the cash flow statement, these transfers are:

options.A: Shown as an investing outflow and an investing inflow
options.B: Shown as a financing outflow and a financing inflow
options.C: Shown as an operating outflow and an operating inflow
options.D: Not shown as cash flows at all, because movements between items that together constitute cash and cash equivalents are a part of the cash management of the enterprise

e: Transfers between a bank account and instruments qualifying as cash equivalents are movements within cash and cash equivalents themselves. They are part of cash management and are not shown as cash flows in the cash flow statement.

q: Where an enterprise issues shares at a premium and the whole amount, including the premium, is received in cash, the source of funds to be shown in the fund flow statement is:

options.A: Only the face value of the shares issued, the premium being ignored
options.B: The total amount received, that is, the face value of the shares together with the securities premium, and not the face value alone
options.C: Only the amount of the securities premium
options.D: The market value of the shares on the date of issue, whether received or not

e: The source of funds on a share issue is the total amount actually received, face value plus securities premium. Showing only the face value would understate the funds generated by the issue in the fund flow statement.

q: In a fund flow statement, the net increase in working capital during a period, as worked out from the schedule of changes in working capital, is shown:

options.A: On the application or uses side of the statement, a net decrease in working capital being correspondingly shown as a source of funds
options.B: On the sources side of the statement in every case
options.C: Only in the profit and loss account of the enterprise
options.D: Nowhere in the statement, since working capital changes are not funds flows

e: A net increase in working capital absorbs funds and is therefore shown on the application or uses side of the fund flow statement. Correspondingly, a net decrease in working capital releases funds and is shown as a source.

q: An important limitation of the fund flow statement is that:

options.A: It cannot be prepared from the published accounts of an enterprise
options.B: It shows the cash position of the enterprise on every day of the year
options.C: It is historical in nature, being prepared from two balance sheets, and it does not by itself disclose the cash or liquidity position of the enterprise, the details of the individual current items appearing only in the separate schedule of changes in working capital
options.D: It is not permitted to be prepared by any enterprise

e: The fund flow statement is historical, being built from two balance sheets, and it does not by itself disclose the cash or liquidity position. The details of individual current items appear only in the separate schedule of changes in working capital.

q: Cost ascertainment, as distinct from cost estimation, refers to:

options.A: Predicting the probable cost of a job in advance, mainly for quoting prices and submitting tenders
options.B: Determining the actual cost of work already performed, collected from the cost records
options.C: Fixing in advance the cost that ought to be incurred under efficient working conditions
options.D: Comparing the actual cost of a period with the budgeted cost for the same period

e: Cost ascertainment means determining the actual cost of work already performed, collected from the cost records. It is distinct from cost estimation, which predicts the probable cost in advance for quotations and tenders.

q: From the following data, the cost of material consumed during a period is: opening stock of raw material Rs 45,000; purchases Rs 2,75,000; carriage inwards Rs 12,000; purchase returns Rs 7,000; closing stock of raw material Rs 60,000:
e: Material consumed = Rs 45,000 + Rs 2,75,000 + Rs 12,000 - Rs 7,000 - Rs 60,000 = Rs 2,65,000. Carriage inwards is added as part of material cost and purchase returns are deducted before deducting the closing stock.

q: Under the HIFO (highest-in, first-out) method of pricing material issues, issues to production are priced at:

options.A: The highest price of the lots of material held in stock, so that the closing stock is left valued at the lowest prices
options.B: The lowest price of the lots of material held in stock, so that issues are charged out as cheaply as possible
options.C: The price of the lot most recently purchased, irrespective of the other lots in stock
options.D: A predetermined standard price fixed for the whole accounting period

e: Under HIFO, issues are priced at the highest price of the lots held in stock. Charging out the costliest lots first leaves the closing stock valued at the lowest prices, a conservative valuation.

q: The annual demand for a material is 6,000 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 75 and the purchase price is Rs 50 per unit. The carrying cost is 20% per annum of the purchase price. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:

options.A: 212 units
options.B: 424 units
options.C: 600 units
options.D: 300 units

e: Carrying cost per unit per year = 20 percent of Rs 50 = Rs 10. EOQ = sqrt(2 x 6,000 x Rs 75 / Rs 10) = sqrt(90,000) = 300 units, the order size that balances ordering and carrying costs.

q: Unit (single output) costing is most suitably applied in concerns which:

options.A: Undertake work strictly according to each customer's separate specification
options.B: Produce a single homogeneous product continuously, such as mines, quarries and brick kilns
options.C: Pass their product through a number of distinct processes before completion
options.D: Render services measured in composite units such as passenger-kilometres

e: Unit or single output costing suits concerns producing a single homogeneous product continuously, such as mines, quarries and brick kilns. Total cost for the period is divided by the units produced to get the cost per unit.

q: The standard variable overhead rate of a department is Rs 12 per hour and the standard hours for the actual output are 4,000. Actual hours worked are 4,400 and the actual variable overheads incurred are Rs 54,000. The variable overhead cost variance is:

options.A: Rs 6,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 1,200 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 4,800 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 6,000 (Favourable)

e: Variable overhead cost variance = standard cost for actual output - actual cost = Rs 12 x 4,000 - Rs 54,000 = Rs 48,000 - Rs 54,000 = Rs 6,000 adverse. Actual overhead exceeds the standard allowed for the output achieved.

q: Under the standard price method of pricing material issues:

options.A: Issues are priced at the actual purchase price of the oldest lot in stock
options.B: Issues are priced at the current market (replacement) price ruling on the date of issue
options.C: Issues are priced at a predetermined standard price, and the difference between the actual purchase price and the standard price is isolated as a price variance
options.D: Issues are priced by adding a fixed percentage to the cost price to cover normal wastage in stores

e: Under the standard price method, issues are priced at a predetermined standard price fixed for the period. The difference between the actual purchase price and the standard price is isolated as a material price variance, keeping issue valuation uniform.

q: Under the Priestman group bonus scheme, the time wages of a group of workers for a week are Rs 40,000. The standard output for the week is 5,000 units, but the group actually produces 6,000 units. The total wages payable to the group for the week are:
e: Output rose by (6,000 - 5,000) / 5,000 = 20 percent, so under the Priestman scheme the group earns a 20 percent bonus on time wages. Total wages = Rs 40,000 + 20 percent of Rs 40,000 = Rs 40,000 + Rs 8,000 = Rs 48,000.

q: In the collection of factory overheads, 'standing order numbers' are:

options.A: The serial numbers allotted to customers' orders when they are received by the factory
options.B: Numbers allotted to each item or source of indirect expenditure, against which overhead costs are collected and classified
options.C: The code numbers allotted to machines for the purpose of computing the machine hour rate
options.D: The numbers allotted to stores items in the priced stores ledger

e: Standing order numbers are numbers allotted to each item or source of indirect expenditure in the factory. Overheads are collected and classified against these numbers, providing a systematic analysis of indirect costs by their cause.

q: The sales budget of a firm provides for the sale of 8,000 units at Rs 55 per unit. Actual sales are 9,500 units at Rs 52 per unit. The total sales variance, computed on the value (turnover) basis, is:

options.A: Rs 54,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 82,500 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 28,500 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 54,000 (Adverse)

e: Actual sales value = 9,500 x Rs 52 = Rs 4,94,000; budgeted sales value = 8,000 x Rs 55 = Rs 4,40,000. Total sales variance on the value basis = Rs 4,94,000 - Rs 4,40,000 = Rs 54,000 favourable, since actual turnover exceeds budget.

q: A 'current standard' in standard costing is a standard which:

options.A: Is set at the level attainable under perfect working conditions, with no allowance for normal wastage or idle time
options.B: Remains unchanged over a long period and is used only to measure trends in costs over the years
options.C: Is fixed once for all by the costing manual and is never revised thereafter
options.D: Is based on current working conditions and prices, and remains in force only for a short period, being revised as conditions change

e: A current standard is based on current working conditions and prices and remains in force only for a short period. It is revised as conditions change, unlike a basic standard kept unchanged for long-term trend measurement or an ideal standard assuming perfect conditions.

q: A worker is paid a piece rate of Rs 15 per unit for the units accepted as good. In a week he produces 320 units, of which 20 units are rejected as defective owing to his own fault. His earnings for the week are:
e: Payment is only for units accepted as good: 320 - 20 = 300 units. Earnings = 300 x Rs 15 = Rs 4,500; units rejected owing to the worker's own fault earn no piece wages.

q: An essential requirement for the successful installation of a costing system in a factory is that:

options.A: The system should be designed to suit the nature, size and working methods of the particular business, and introduced with the cooperation of the departments concerned
options.B: A ready-made system working successfully in another factory should be adopted without any change
options.C: The costing department should work in complete isolation from the production departments
options.D: The maximum possible number of forms and returns should be introduced from the very beginning

e: A costing system succeeds only if it is designed to suit the nature, size and working methods of the particular business and is introduced with the cooperation of the departments concerned. A ready-made system copied without change, or one run in isolation, does not work.

q: From the following data for a period, the cost of sales is: raw material consumed Rs 4,00,000; direct labour Rs 2,00,000; direct expenses Rs 40,000; factory overheads Rs 1,60,000; opening work-in-progress Rs 60,000; closing work-in-progress Rs 40,000; administration overheads Rs 1,10,000; opening stock of finished goods Rs 70,000; closing stock of finished goods Rs 50,000; selling and distribution overheads Rs 50,000:
e: Works cost = Rs 4,00,000 + Rs 2,00,000 + Rs 40,000 + Rs 1,60,000 + Rs 60,000 - Rs 40,000 = Rs 8,20,000. Adding administration Rs 1,10,000 and finished goods stock adjustment Rs 70,000 - Rs 50,000 gives Rs 9,50,000, and adding selling overheads Rs 50,000 gives cost of sales Rs 10,00,000.

q: The main purpose of an idle time card in a factory is to:

options.A: Record the time at which each worker enters and leaves the factory gate
options.B: Record the time spent by each worker on each job and operation performed by him
options.C: Fix the standard time allowed for each job undertaken in the factory
options.D: Record separately, under its cause, the time for which workers were paid but no production took place, so that idle time can be analysed and controlled

e: An idle time card records separately, under its cause, the time for which workers were paid but no production took place. This analysis of idle time by cause enables management to control avoidable idle time; gate time and job time are recorded on other records.

q: The contract price of a work is Rs 60,00,000. The value of work certified is Rs 24,00,000, that is, 40% of the contract price, and the notional profit on the contract to date is Rs 1,35,000. Cash received from the contractee is 80% of the work certified. Using the rule applicable where work certified is between one-fourth and one-half of the contract price, the profit to be credited to the Profit and Loss Account is:
e: Work certified is 40 percent of the contract price, between one-fourth and one-half, so one-third of notional profit adjusted for cash is credited. Profit to Profit and Loss Account = 1/3 x Rs 1,35,000 x 80 percent = Rs 36,000.

q: Under the base stock method of pricing material issues, the base stock, being a fixed minimum quantity of material always held in stores, is:

options.A: Treated practically as a fixed asset and always valued at the price at which it was first received, issues above the base quantity being priced on the FIFO or a similar basis
options.B: Revalued at the current market price at the end of every accounting period
options.C: Written off entirely to production in the year in which it is first created
options.D: Valued at the highest price paid for any lot during the year

e: Under the base stock method, the fixed minimum base stock is treated practically as a fixed asset and is always valued at the price at which it was first received. Issues above the base quantity are priced on the FIFO or a similar basis.

q: Under activity-based costing, the machine set-up cost pool of a plant is Rs 3,60,000 for 1,800 set-ups and the quality inspection cost pool is Rs 1,40,000 for 2,800 inspections. A product requires 250 set-ups and 400 inspections. The total overhead cost assigned to the product is:
e: Set-up rate = Rs 3,60,000 / 1,800 = Rs 200 per set-up, giving 250 x Rs 200 = Rs 50,000. Inspection rate = Rs 1,40,000 / 2,800 = Rs 50 per inspection, giving 400 x Rs 50 = Rs 20,000, so total overhead assigned = Rs 70,000.

q: In a factory, overtime has to be worked because production was held up by a flood and a breakdown of power supply, both abnormal circumstances. The overtime premium payable for this work should be charged to:

options.A: The jobs on which the workers happened to be engaged during the overtime hours
options.B: The factory overheads of the period, to be absorbed by all jobs of the period
options.C: The customer who placed the largest order during that week
options.D: The Costing Profit and Loss Account, as an abnormal loss

e: Overtime premium caused by abnormal circumstances such as a flood and a power breakdown is not a normal cost of any job or of the period's production. It is charged to the Costing Profit and Loss Account as an abnormal loss.

q: The budgeted sales of two products are: A — 4,000 units and B — 2,000 units, the standard margins being Rs 25 per unit for A and Rs 15 per unit for B. The total quantity actually sold is 6,600 units. The sales quantity variance, computed on the margin basis, is:

options.A: Rs 13,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 10,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 3,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 15,000 (Favourable)

e: In standard mix, actual total sales of 6,600 units give revised quantities A = 4,400 and B = 2,200 against budgets of 4,000 and 2,000. Quantity variance = (4,400 - 4,000) x Rs 25 + (2,200 - 2,000) x Rs 15 = Rs 10,000 + Rs 3,000 = Rs 13,000 favourable.

q: In the three-variance method of analysing the total overhead variance, the total overhead variance is analysed into:

options.A: Material price variance, material usage variance and material mix variance
options.B: Labour rate variance, labour efficiency variance and idle time variance
options.C: Spending (budget) variance, efficiency variance and idle capacity (volume) variance
options.D: Sales price variance, sales volume variance and sales mix variance

e: In the three-variance method, the total overhead variance is analysed into the spending or budget variance, the efficiency variance and the idle capacity or volume variance. Together these explain the difference between overheads absorbed and overheads incurred.

q: In a process, the opening work-in-progress is 1,000 units. During the period 6,000 units are completed and transferred to the next process, and the closing work-in-progress is 1,500 units, which are 40% complete as to conversion cost. The equivalent production in respect of conversion cost, computed under the average (weighted average) cost method, is:

options.A: 6,000 units
options.B: 6,600 units
options.C: 7,500 units
options.D: 6,300 units

e: Under the weighted average method, equivalent production for conversion = completed units + closing work-in-progress equivalent = 6,000 + 1,500 x 40 percent = 6,000 + 600 = 6,600 units. Opening work-in-progress is not deducted under this method.

q: In contract costing, plant that was issued to a contract site is returned to stores during the year. The Contract Account is credited with:

options.A: The original cost of the plant when it was purchased
options.B: Nil, because plant once charged to a contract is never credited back
options.C: The estimated scrap value of the plant at the end of its life
options.D: The written-down (depreciated) value of the plant on the date of its return

e: Plant returned from a contract site to stores is credited to the Contract Account at its written-down or depreciated value on the date of return. Crediting original cost would ignore the depreciation for the period the plant was used on the contract.

q: The expected selling price of a new product is Rs 950 per unit and the firm requires a profit margin of 20% on the selling price. The cost of the product, as presently estimated, is Rs 835 per unit. The target cost gap to be eliminated before the product is launched is:

options.A: Rs 75 per unit
options.B: Rs 115 per unit
options.C: Rs 190 per unit
options.D: Rs 60 per unit

e: Target cost = Rs 950 - 20 percent of Rs 950 = Rs 950 - Rs 190 = Rs 760 per unit. Target cost gap = estimated cost Rs 835 - Rs 760 = Rs 75 per unit, which must be eliminated before launch.

q: A duration driver, as distinct from a transaction driver, in activity-based costing measures:

options.A: The number of times an activity is performed, such as the number of purchase orders placed
options.B: The total cost of the resources consumed by the activity during the period
options.C: The amount of time taken to perform the activity, such as set-up hours, rather than merely the number of times the activity occurs
options.D: The selling value of the output for which the activity is performed

e: A duration driver measures the amount of time taken to perform an activity, such as set-up hours, and is used where the time per occurrence varies. A transaction driver merely counts the number of times the activity occurs, such as the number of set-ups.

q: The closing stock of a receiving process is valued at Rs 90,000. The output was transferred to it by the earlier process at cost plus 25% on cost. The unrealised profit included in the closing stock, for which a stock reserve is to be created, is:
e: Transfer price is cost plus 25 percent on cost, so profit is 25/125 of the transfer value. Unrealised profit in closing stock = Rs 90,000 x 25/125 = Rs 18,000, for which a stock reserve is created against the inter-process profit.

q: A product line shows: sales Rs 6,00,000; variable costs Rs 3,90,000; fixed costs specifically attributable to the line and avoidable if it is dropped Rs 1,50,000; allocated common fixed costs Rs 1,10,000; and a reported net loss of Rs 50,000. If the line is dropped, the total profit of the firm will:

options.A: Increase by Rs 50,000
options.B: Decrease by Rs 2,10,000
options.C: Remain unchanged
options.D: Decrease by Rs 60,000

e: Contribution of the line = Rs 6,00,000 - Rs 3,90,000 = Rs 2,10,000, and its segment margin after avoidable fixed costs = Rs 2,10,000 - Rs 1,50,000 = Rs 60,000. Dropping it loses this Rs 60,000 while allocated common fixed costs continue, so total profit falls by Rs 60,000 despite the reported loss.

q: 'Generic benchmarking', as a technique of performance improvement, involves:

options.A: Comparing a business process with the best practice of that process wherever it is found, even in a completely unrelated industry
options.B: Comparing the performance of one department or unit with another unit of the same organisation
options.C: Comparing the firm's products and costs only with those of its direct competitors
options.D: Comparing a function of the firm with the same function in another firm of the same industry

e: Generic benchmarking compares a business process with the best practice of that process wherever it is found, even in a completely unrelated industry. It looks beyond competitors and the firm's own industry for the best way of performing the process.

q: The estimated works cost of a job is Rs 3,00,000. Office and administration overheads are to be recovered at 10% of works cost, and a profit of 20% on the selling price is required. The price to be quoted for the job is:
e: Cost of production = Rs 3,00,000 + 10 percent of Rs 3,00,000 = Rs 3,30,000. Profit is 20 percent on selling price, so quoted price = Rs 3,30,000 / (1 - 0.20) = Rs 3,30,000 / 0.80 = Rs 4,12,500.

q: In contract costing, the amounts paid to sub-contractors for work executed by them as part of the main contract are:

options.A: Treated as a part of the cost of materials issued to the contract
options.B: Debited directly to the Contract Account as a charge for work done on the contract
options.C: Borne by the main contractor personally and not charged to the contract at all
options.D: Apportioned as general overheads over all the contracts in hand

e: Amounts paid to sub-contractors for work executed as part of the main contract are a direct charge on that contract. They are debited directly to the Contract Account, like other contract costs, and not treated as materials or general overheads.

q: Pareto analysis, as applied to inventory control and cost control, is based on the observation that:

options.A: All items of stores contribute equally to the total value of inventory
options.B: Total cost increases in a straight line with the level of output
options.C: Defects in production occur evenly over all products and processes
options.D: A small proportion of the items accounts for a large proportion of the total value, the 'vital few', while the remaining large number of items accounts for only a small proportion, the 'trivial many'

e: Pareto analysis rests on the observation that a small proportion of items, the vital few, accounts for a large proportion of total value, while the large remaining number, the trivial many, accounts for only a small proportion. Control effort is therefore concentrated on the vital few.

q: A contract is nearing completion. The contract price is Rs 80,00,000 and the estimated total cost of the contract is Rs 68,00,000. The value of work certified is Rs 60,00,000 and cash received from the contractee is Rs 54,00,000. On the estimated profit basis, the profit to be credited to the Profit and Loss Account is:
The first unit of a new product takes 400 labour hours. The learning rate is 90%. The cumulative average labour time per unit for the first four units is:

options.A: 360 hours
options.B: 400 hours
options.C: 324 hours
options.D: 288 hours

e: With a 90 percent learning rate, the cumulative average time halves in ratio at each doubling: for 2 units it is 400 x 0.90 = 360 hours, and for 4 units 360 x 0.90 = 324 hours per unit.

q: Under the reverse cost method of accounting for a by-product, the value at which the by-product is credited to the process account is arrived at by:

options.A: Adding the estimated profit margin to the cost of further processing of the by-product
options.B: Deducting from the sales value of the by-product the estimated profit margin on it, its selling and distribution expenses and the cost of its further processing after the split-off point, and crediting the net amount to the process
options.C: Crediting the full gross sales value of the by-product to the process account without any deduction
options.D: Ignoring the by-product altogether until the whole of it is sold

e: Under the reverse cost method, the credit to the process is the sales value of the by-product minus its estimated profit margin, its selling and distribution expenses and the cost of further processing after the split-off point. Only this net amount is credited to the process account.

q: A firm sells two products in a constant sales mix (by value): Product A — sales Rs 4,00,000 with a P/V ratio of 50%, and Product B — sales Rs 6,00,000 with a P/V ratio of 30%. Total fixed costs are Rs 5,70,000. The overall break-even sales of the firm are:
e: Weighted contribution = Rs 4,00,000 x 50 percent + Rs 6,00,000 x 30 percent = Rs 2,00,000 + Rs 1,80,000 = Rs 3,80,000 on sales of Rs 10,00,000, an overall P/V ratio of 38 percent. Break-even sales = Rs 5,70,000 / 0.38 = Rs 15,00,000.

q: The method of least squares, used for segregating a semi-variable cost into its fixed and variable elements, is regarded as the most accurate statistical method because it:

options.A: Fits the cost line by using all the observations and minimising the sum of the squares of the deviations of the observations from that line
options.B: Uses only the observations at the highest and the lowest levels of activity
options.C: Fits the cost line by visual inspection of the observations plotted on a graph
options.D: Uses only the budgeted figures for the coming year and ignores past data

e: The least squares method fits the cost line using all the observations and minimising the sum of the squares of the deviations of the observations from the line. Using every observation, rather than only two points or visual fitting, makes it the most accurate statistical method.

q: Under the survey (points) method of apportioning joint costs among joint products, the joint costs are apportioned on the basis of:

options.A: The physical quantities of the joint products obtained
options.B: The sales values of the joint products at the split-off point
options.C: Points or weights assigned to each product after a survey of factors such as its grade and quality, the difficulty of its production and its market value
options.D: The further processing costs incurred on each product after the split-off point

e: Under the survey or points method, joint costs are apportioned on points or weights assigned to each product after a survey of factors such as grade and quality, difficulty of production and market value. It is used where physical quantities or sales values alone would be unfair bases.

q: A firm sells a product at Rs 120 per unit, its variable cost being Rs 64 per unit and its fixed costs Rs 3,60,000. It proposes to reduce the selling price to Rs 100 per unit. The number of units it must sell at the reduced price to maintain its present profit of Rs 1,80,000 is:

options.A: 12,000 units
options.B: 15,000 units
options.C: 13,500 units
options.D: 18,000 units

e: Contribution needed = fixed costs + target profit = Rs 3,60,000 + Rs 1,80,000 = Rs 5,40,000. New contribution per unit = Rs 100 - Rs 64 = Rs 36, so units required = Rs 5,40,000 / Rs 36 = 15,000 units at the reduced price.

q: Where a plant making both high-volume standard products and low-volume complex products absorbs overheads by a traditional volume-based rate (such as direct labour hours), the usual result is that:

options.A: Both classes of products are costed with equal accuracy
options.B: The low-volume complex products are over-costed and the high-volume products are under-costed
options.C: Overhead absorption has no effect on the relative profitability of the products
options.D: The high-volume standard products are over-costed and the low-volume complex products are under-costed, the former thus cross-subsidising the latter

e: A volume-based rate such as direct labour hours loads overheads in proportion to volume, so high-volume standard products absorb too much overhead and low-volume complex products too little. The high-volume products are thus over-costed and cross-subsidise the complex ones, distorting relative profitability.

q: The installed capacity of a plant is 25,000 units. A product sells at Rs 160 per unit, its variable cost is Rs 100 per unit and the fixed costs are Rs 12,60,000. The profit when the plant works at 90% of its installed capacity is:
e: Output at 90 percent capacity = 25,000 x 0.90 = 22,500 units. Contribution = 22,500 x (Rs 160 - Rs 100) = 22,500 x Rs 60 = Rs 13,50,000, and profit = Rs 13,50,000 - Rs 12,60,000 = Rs 90,000.

q: Which of the following is a support (secondary) activity in Porter's value chain analysis?

options.A: Inbound logistics
options.B: Operations
options.C: Procurement
options.D: Marketing and sales

e: In Porter's value chain, inbound logistics, operations and marketing and sales are primary activities directly concerned with making and selling the product. Procurement is a support or secondary activity that assists the primary activities.

q: In a process, 5,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 2,40,000. Normal loss is 10% of input and the scrap realises Rs 30 per unit. The actual output obtained is 4,650 units. The value of the abnormal gain is:
e: Expected output = 5,000 - 10 percent normal loss = 4,500 units. Net cost = Rs 2,40,000 - 500 x Rs 30 scrap = Rs 2,25,000, so cost per unit = Rs 2,25,000 / 4,500 = Rs 50. Abnormal gain = (4,650 - 4,500) x Rs 50 = 150 x Rs 50 = Rs 7,500.

q: A firm that follows 'cost leadership' as its generic (strategic positioning) strategy seeks competitive advantage primarily by:

options.A: Charging the highest price in the industry for a unique product
options.B: Offering features that no competitor can imitate, whatever the cost
options.C: Concentrating all its resources on one narrow market segment only
options.D: Becoming the lowest-cost producer in the industry while offering a product of a quality acceptable to buyers

e: A cost leadership strategy seeks competitive advantage by becoming the lowest-cost producer in the industry while offering a product of acceptable quality. The cost advantage, not a premium price or a narrow segment, is the basis of competition.

q: Two alternative processes are available for making a component. Process X involves fixed costs of Rs 1,80,000 and a variable cost of Rs 35 per unit. Process Y involves fixed costs of Rs 4,20,000 and a variable cost of Rs 15 per unit. The cost indifference point between the two processes is:

options.A: 12,000 units
options.B: 8,000 units
options.C: 16,000 units
options.D: 10,000 units

e: At the indifference point the total costs are equal: Rs 1,80,000 + Rs 35x = Rs 4,20,000 + Rs 15x, so Rs 20x = Rs 2,40,000 and x = 12,000 units. Below this volume the low-fixed-cost process is cheaper, and above it the low-variable-cost process is cheaper.

q: The quality costs of a factory for a period are: prevention costs Rs 1,50,000; appraisal costs Rs 90,000; internal failure costs Rs 70,000; external failure costs Rs 1,10,000. The cost of conformance for the period is:
e: Cost of conformance = prevention costs + appraisal costs = Rs 1,50,000 + Rs 90,000 = Rs 2,40,000. These are the costs incurred to ensure quality is achieved; internal and external failure costs together form the cost of non-conformance.

q: A lease rental of Rs 60,000 is payable at the beginning of each year for 3 years. At a discount rate of 10%, the present value factor for an annuity due of 3 years is 2.736. The present value of the lease rentals is:
e: Present value of the annuity due = Rs 60,000 x 2.736 = Rs 1,64,160. The given factor already reflects payment at the beginning of each year, so it is applied directly to the annual rental.

q: For the same amount, term and discount rate, the present value of an annuity due (payments at the beginning of each period) is higher than that of an ordinary annuity (payments at the end of each period) because:

options.A: The annuity due has one extra payment
options.B: No discounting is applied to an annuity due
options.C: Each payment of the annuity due is discounted for one period less
options.D: A lower discount rate is prescribed for an annuity due

e: Each payment of an annuity due is received one period earlier and is therefore discounted for one period less than the corresponding payment of an ordinary annuity. With the same amount, term and rate, this makes the present value of the annuity due higher.

q: An enterprise deposits Rs 2,00,000 at the end of each year for 4 years in a sinking fund earning 10% per annum compound interest. The future value annuity factor for 4 years at 10% is 4.641. The amount accumulated in the fund at the end of 4 years is:
e: Accumulated amount = Rs 2,00,000 x 4.641 = Rs 9,28,200. The future value annuity factor compounds each end-of-year deposit at 10 percent to the end of the fourth year.

q: A sinking fund in financial management is best described as a fund built up by periodic deposits, accumulating with interest, in order to:

options.A: Meet day-to-day working capital needs
options.B: Pay the annual interest on debentures
options.C: Distribute bonus shares to shareholders
options.D: Replace an asset or redeem a liability at a future date

e: A sinking fund is built up by periodic deposits accumulating with interest for a specific future purpose. That purpose is to replace an asset or redeem a liability, such as debentures, at a future date, not to meet day-to-day needs.

q: A loan of Rs 9,51,000 is to be repaid in 4 equal annual instalments at the end of each year. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at the interest rate charged is 3.170. The amount of each annual instalment is:
e: Annual instalment = loan / annuity factor = Rs 9,51,000 / 3.170 = Rs 3,00,000. Equal end-of-year instalments of this amount have a present value exactly equal to the loan.

q: In the amortisation of a loan repaid in equal annual instalments, as the years pass:

options.A: The interest component rises and the principal component falls
options.B: The interest component falls and the principal component rises
options.C: Both components remain equal throughout
options.D: The whole instalment is interest in the first half and principal in the second half

e: In an equal-instalment amortisation, interest is charged on the falling outstanding balance, so the interest component falls each year. Since the instalment is constant, the principal component rises correspondingly over the loan period.

q: A loan carries interest at a nominal rate of 12% per annum, compounded quarterly. Its effective annual rate of interest, computed as (1.03)^4 - 1, is:
e: Effective annual rate = (1 + 0.12/4) to the power 4 - 1 = (1.03) to the power 4 - 1 = 1.1255 - 1 = 12.55 percent. Quarterly compounding makes the effective rate higher than the nominal 12 percent.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 9,00,000 and yields total net cash inflows of Rs 15,30,000 over its life. Its post-payback profitability (total inflows minus the initial outlay) is:
e: Post-payback profitability = total net cash inflows - initial outlay = Rs 15,30,000 - Rs 9,00,000 = Rs 6,30,000. It measures the surplus earned over the whole life after the outlay has been recovered in the payback period.

q: The post-payback profitability index of a project is computed as:

options.A: Post-payback profitability divided by the initial outlay
options.B: Initial outlay divided by the total cash inflows
options.C: Post-payback profitability divided by the total cash inflows
options.D: Total cash inflows divided by the payback period

e: The post-payback profitability index = post-payback profitability / initial outlay. Expressing the post-recovery surplus relative to the original investment allows projects of different sizes to be compared.

q: A project is expected to yield a profit before interest and tax of Rs 5,00,000 in a year. Depreciation on the project assets is Rs 1,00,000 and the tax rate is 30%. The cash flow after tax for the year is:
e: Cash flow after tax = Rs 5,00,000 - 30 percent of Rs 5,00,000 + Rs 1,00,000 depreciation = Rs 5,00,000 - Rs 1,50,000 + Rs 1,00,000 = Rs 4,50,000. Depreciation is a non-cash charge and is added back after computing tax on the profit.

q: An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 10,00,000 and a tax rate of 30%. During the year it incurs depreciation of Rs 2,00,000, capital expenditure of Rs 3,50,000 and an increase in working capital of Rs 50,000. Its free cash flow to the firm is:
e: Free cash flow to the firm = Rs 10,00,000 x (1 - 0.30) + Rs 2,00,000 - Rs 3,50,000 - Rs 50,000 = Rs 7,00,000 + Rs 2,00,000 - Rs 4,00,000 = Rs 5,00,000. Depreciation is added back, while capital expenditure and the working capital increase are deducted.

q: The free cash flow of an enterprise, in essence, represents the cash that:

options.A: Is available for distribution to all providers of capital after meeting operating expenses, tax, capital expenditure and working capital needs
options.B: Remains in the cash book at the end of the year
options.C: Is available only for payment of dividend to equity shareholders
options.D: The enterprise receives from the issue of fresh share capital

e: Free cash flow is the cash available for distribution to all providers of capital, debt and equity together. It is what remains after meeting operating expenses, tax, capital expenditure and working capital needs.

q: The expected net cash inflow of a project in a year is Rs 5,00,000 and its certainty-equivalent coefficient is 0.80. The risk-free discount factor for that year is 0.909. The present value of the inflow under the certainty-equivalent method is:
e: Certainty-equivalent inflow = Rs 5,00,000 x 0.80 = Rs 4,00,000. Present value = Rs 4,00,000 x 0.909 = Rs 3,63,600, discounting the risk-adjusted certain amount at the risk-free rate rather than discounting the risky amount at a risk-adjusted rate.

q: In the certainty-equivalent method, the certainty-equivalent coefficient of a cash flow will be lower when:

options.A: The cash flow is receivable earlier
options.B: The perceived risk of the cash flow is greater
options.C: The discount rate is lower
options.D: The project life is shorter

e: The certainty-equivalent coefficient expresses a risky cash flow as a fraction of its certain equivalent, so it falls as the perceived risk of the cash flow rises. A riskier flow is worth less with certainty, giving a lower coefficient, always between zero and one.

q: A project requires an outlay of Rs 12,00,000. A decision-tree appraisal shows two outcomes: with probability 0.6, inflows with a present value of Rs 20,00,000, and with probability 0.4, inflows with a present value of Rs 8,00,000. The expected net present value of the project is:
e: Expected present value of inflows = 0.6 x Rs 20,00,000 + 0.4 x Rs 8,00,000 = Rs 12,00,000 + Rs 3,20,000 = Rs 15,20,000. Expected NPV = Rs 15,20,000 - Rs 12,00,000 = Rs 3,20,000, probability-weighting the outcomes shown by the decision tree.
